title: WHY DID GOD ALLOW EZEKIEL TO USE LANGUAGE SO SHOCKING THAT MANY CHURCHES WON’T EVEN READ IT ALOUD?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD ALLOW EZEKIEL TO USE LANGUAGE SO SHOCKING THAT MANY CHURCHES WON’T EVEN READ IT ALOUD?

Ezekiel 23 is one of the Bible’s most disturbing chapters. But beneath its graphic language lies a terrifying revelation about spiritual betrayal, the patience of God, and the devastating cost of giving your heart to everything except the One who loves you.
There are chapters in the Bible that comfort you.
There are chapters that strengthen you.
And then there are chapters that make you stop reading, stare at the page, and wonder...
“Did God really say that?”
Ezekiel 23 is one of those chapters.
It contains language so sexually explicit, accusations so humiliating, and images so disturbing that many Christians have never heard the entire chapter read from a pulpit.
Some believers encounter it for the first time and feel genuinely shocked.
Others wonder why such language belongs in a holy book.
And some quietly ask a question they are almost afraid to say aloud.
“Why would God speak about His own people like this?”
But perhaps the most important question is not why the chapter makes us uncomfortable.
Perhaps it is why the sins being exposed had become so comfortable to the people committing them.
Because Ezekiel 23 was never written to entertain an audience with scandal.
It was a prophetic indictment of a people who had repeatedly exchanged covenant faithfulness for idolatry, political dependence, and spiritual rebellion.
And when you understand what was happening behind those shocking words, something changes.
You stop reading merely as a spectator of ancient Israel's failure.
You begin examining the things competing for your own heart.
And that is where this chapter becomes painfully personal.
Imagine someone who has loved you faithfully.
Someone who rescued you when you had nothing.
Someone who provided for you, protected you, and remained patient through repeated betrayal.
Now imagine that instead of responding with gratitude, you continually turn toward those who exploit you.
You pursue them.
You trust their promises.
You surrender your loyalty.
And when everything collapses, you return to the one who loved you, not necessarily because you have changed, but because you need rescuing again.
Then, once you recover, you repeat the betrayal.
How long could such a relationship continue without a reckoning?
That question helps us understand the emotional and covenantal background of Ezekiel 23.
But we must be careful.

This chapter is not permission to humiliate an unfaithful spouse, degrade women, or justify abuse. Its disturbing sexual imagery belongs to a specific prophetic literary form addressing nations, kingdoms, and their covenant violations.
The prophet is not offering ordinary marriage counseling.
He is announcing divine judgment against entrenched national unfaithfulness.
And the language is deliberately difficult.
The chapter begins:
“Son of man, there were two women, the daughters of one mother.” — Ezekiel 23:2, KJV
These two symbolic sisters are named Oholah and Oholibah.
Their names are not incidental.
In the Hebrew text, the first is אָהֳלָה (Oholah), commonly understood as “her tent.”
The second is אָהֳלִיבָה (Oholibah), commonly understood as “my tent is in her.”
The Hebrew word אֹהֶל (ohel) means “tent,” a word that can carry associations with dwelling and, in biblical worship, the tabernacle.
These names are part of the prophecy's message.
Ezekiel identifies Oholah with Samaria, representing the northern kingdom of Israel, and Oholibah with Jerusalem, representing the southern kingdom of Judah.
“My tent is in her” is especially significant in connection with Jerusalem, the city where God's temple stood.
Jerusalem possessed extraordinary religious privilege.
The temple.
The priesthood.
The sacrifices.
The covenant history.
The memory of God's mighty acts.
Yet the presence of sacred institutions did not guarantee a faithful heart.
You can be surrounded by the things of God and still give your deepest allegiance to something else.
That was Jerusalem's tragedy.
And it remains a warning for religious people today.
A person can attend worship every week and still live under the control of greed.
A person can quote Scripture and still cultivate cruelty.
A person can speak passionately about holiness while hiding patterns of dishonesty.
A person can defend the reputation of a church while refusing to confront injustice within it.
The appearance of devotion is not the same as devotion itself.
But Ezekiel's accusation was even more specific.
Israel and Judah were not simply failing to maintain a private religious feeling.
They were turning toward foreign powers, adopting idolatrous practices, participating in corrupt worship, and trusting political alliances in ways that contradicted their covenant obligations.
The prophet describes their conduct through an extended metaphor of sexual infidelity.
The Hebrew word זָנָה (zanah) is important here.
Its basic sense concerns prostitution or sexual unfaithfulness. In prophetic literature, it is frequently used figuratively for idolatry and covenant betrayal.
That distinction matters.
Ezekiel is not claiming that every sexual image in the chapter represents a literal sexual act committed by the entire population.
He is using sexual betrayal as a metaphor for religious and political infidelity.
The shocking imagery is designed to expose how seriously Judah's conduct violated its covenant relationship with God.
Oholah, the northern kingdom, became entangled with Assyria.
Historically, Samaria fell to Assyria in 722/721 BC.
Her destruction was not a theoretical warning.
It had already happened.
Judah had witnessed the collapse of its northern sister.
Jerusalem knew the history.
Jerusalem had seen the consequences.
And still, according to Ezekiel, she repeated and intensified the pattern.
Think about that.
It is one thing to stumble because you do not understand the danger.
It is another to watch someone else fall into a destructive pattern, recognize the consequences, and still convince yourself that your own outcome will somehow be different.
That is not merely ancient history.
That is human nature.
We watch pride destroy relationships, yet defend our own arrogance.
We watch greed consume families, yet tell ourselves one more compromise will finally make us secure.
We watch bitterness poison someone else's life, yet quietly feed our own resentment.
We watch spiritual neglect hollow out a person's faith, yet keep postponing prayer, repentance, and obedience.
We see the warning.
We understand the danger.
And somehow we still believe we are the exception.
Jerusalem did.
Then Ezekiel's language becomes even more disturbing.
In verse 20, the prophet uses an explicit comparison involving the sexual anatomy and emissions of animals.
The Hebrew text is graphic. Responsible translations should not pretend otherwise.
The passage uses sexual excess as an image of Jerusalem's consuming desire for foreign powers, particularly Egypt.
Its purpose is not to provide erotic detail for the reader's enjoyment.
It is to portray Judah's disordered loyalties in deliberately repellent terms.
The imagery is meant to shock.
But shock is not the same thing as understanding.
And it is possible to recognize the prophet's purpose without pretending the imagery is easy, or that every modern reader will experience it in the same way.
Some readers, especially survivors of sexual violence or humiliation, may find the chapter deeply distressing.
That reaction should not be dismissed.
Faithful interpretation requires both honesty about the text and compassion toward the people reading it.
The chapter's violent descriptions of judgment must never be turned into permission for believers to shame, threaten, or abuse anyone.
Ezekiel is describing divine judgment through an ancient prophetic allegory.
He is not instructing Christians to imitate its violence.
Yet underneath the unsettling language is a devastating theological accusation.
God's people were seeking security, satisfaction, and identity from powers that could not save them.
They had become fascinated with what would ultimately destroy them.
And that is one of sin's oldest strategies.
Sin rarely introduces itself as destruction. It usually arrives disguised as something you cannot live without.
It promises freedom.
Then it demands obedience.
It promises comfort.
Then it becomes a dependency.
It promises belonging.
Then it pressures you to compromise your convictions.
It promises control.
Then it begins controlling you.
And eventually, the thing you once pursued for security becomes the very thing you fear losing.
This does not mean every painful dependency, trauma response, or personal struggle is equivalent to Judah's deliberate national rebellion.
Scripture does not flatten every human wound into the same moral category.
But the chapter does invite us to examine where our trust and allegiance have gone.
What do you turn to when you feel empty?
What receives the loyalty that belongs to God?
What compromise have you begun calling normal because confronting it would require change?
What truth have you avoided because you already know what obedience would cost?
These are uncomfortable questions.
But they are not asked to drive you into despair.
They are asked because repentance begins when we stop defending what is destroying us.
And then comes one of the most haunting statements in the chapter.
Ezekiel 23:35 declares:
“Because thou hast forgotten me, and cast me behind thy back, therefore bear thou also thy lewdness and thy whoredoms.” — KJV
Listen carefully to the central accusation.
“Thou hast forgotten me, and cast me behind thy back.”
The Hebrew phrase וַתַּשְׁלִיכִי אוֹתִי אַחֲרֵי גַוֵּךְ (vattashlikhi oti acharei gavvekh) communicates the idea of casting God behind one's back.
This is more than a momentary lapse of memory.
It describes treating God as someone who no longer deserves attention or allegiance.
The issue was not that Judah had forgotten God's name.
The people still possessed their religious identity.
The temple still stood for much of the period being condemned.
Religious language had not disappeared.
But their conduct revealed a catastrophic displacement of loyalty.
They had pushed God behind them.
And that should make every religious heart tremble.
Because it is possible to remember the vocabulary of faith while losing the posture of surrender.
It is possible to know the songs without listening to the Lord.
It is possible to defend Christian traditions while resisting Christ's commands.
It is possible to say “God comes first” while organizing your entire life around something else.
Jesus would later confront a similar disconnect between religious appearance and inward devotion.
In Matthew 15:8, He says:
“This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.” — KJV
Jesus was citing Isaiah's prophetic warning.
Different historical circumstances.
The same devastating possibility.
Lips that honor God.
Hearts that wander from Him.
And here is where we must resist an easy mistake.
It would be convenient to read Ezekiel 23 and say, “Those people were terrible.”
It would be comfortable to turn their failures into a lesson about someone else's hypocrisy.
But Scripture was not preserved merely so that later generations could congratulate themselves for being better than their ancestors.
Romans 15:4 reminds us that what was written before was written for our learning.
The point is not to pretend every detail of Judah's history directly describes your life.
The point is to receive the warning rather than stand above it.
Because the human heart still knows how to manufacture substitutes for God.
Some substitutes look obviously sinful.
Others look respectable.
Success can become an idol.
Approval can become an idol.
Money can become an idol.
Religious influence can become an idol.
Even ministry can become an idol when the work of God becomes more important to us than obedience to God.
A person can spend years building a platform about Jesus while quietly neglecting prayer, integrity, compassion, and the people entrusted to their care.
A church can become so concerned with maintaining an image of spiritual success that it begins hiding the very sins it should be confronting.
And a believer can become so practiced at explaining away compromise that repentance starts feeling unnecessary.
That is a frightening place to live.
Not because God's grace has become weak.
But because self-deception can make us resistant to the grace we desperately need.
Now consider the historical weight of Ezekiel's warning.
The prophet ministered during the crisis surrounding Jerusalem's final years and the Babylonian exile.
Judah's leaders had repeatedly looked toward political alliances and foreign powers for security.
Jerusalem's destruction in 586 BC would expose the catastrophic failure of that confidence.
The temple would be burned.
The city would be devastated.
Many people would suffer death, displacement, and exile.
Ezekiel's prophecy belongs to that terrifying historical setting.
It should never be reduced to a vague motivational slogan.
Real people suffered.
Real communities collapsed.
And the biblical narrative places these events within the larger story of covenant judgment.
But the story of Ezekiel does not end in chapter 23.
And this is where the Gospel begins to illuminate the darkness without erasing the seriousness of the warning.
Because if all we hear is judgment, we have not yet listened to the whole prophetic book.
After announcing the consequences of Judah's rebellion, Ezekiel also records astonishing promises of restoration.
In Ezekiel 36:26, God declares:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.” — KJV
Read that again.
“A new heart also will I give you.”
Not merely better appearances.
Not simply improved religious performance.
Not a more convincing public reputation.
A new heart.
The Hebrew phrase לֵב חָדָשׁ (lev chadash) means “a new heart.”
In biblical thought, the heart is not merely the seat of emotions. It is deeply associated with thought, desire, intention, and moral direction.
God was promising a transformation that went deeper than outward conformity.
He would renew His people from within.
And Ezekiel 36:27 goes further:
“And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes...” — KJV
Do you see the movement?
Ezekiel 23 exposes the betrayal.
Ezekiel 36 promises renewal.
The same prophetic book that refuses to minimize sin also refuses to leave restoration out of view.
God's holiness is not compromised by His mercy.
And His mercy is not evidence that sin was harmless.
The promise of a new heart is meaningful precisely because the old heart's condition was so serious.
But how would that promise find its fullest meaning?
The New Testament directs our attention to Jesus Christ.
Not because Ezekiel 23 is secretly a coded prediction of every detail of Jesus' earthly ministry.
It is not.
Its immediate subject is the covenant infidelity and judgment of Samaria and Jerusalem.
But within the wider biblical story, Ezekiel's promise of cleansing, renewed hearts, and God's Spirit prepares us to understand the salvation accomplished through Christ.
Jesus came into a world that had not solved the problem of sin.
Religious knowledge had not solved it.
Political strength had not solved it.
Human determination had not solved it.
And no amount of outward respectability could cleanse the conscience or reconcile sinners to God.
Jesus came not merely to expose our need.
He came to save.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God willingly gave Himself for sinners.
He did not become morally guilty.
He bore our sins in His sacrificial death.
He endured the cross, rose from the dead, and opened the way for forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
The apostle Paul writes:
And Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not wait for sinners to make themselves worthy of rescue.
He came because sinners could not rescue themselves.
And yet His grace does not teach us to remain comfortably enslaved to the very sins from which He came to deliver us.
Grace forgives.
Grace restores.
Grace trains us to renounce ungodliness.
Grace produces a changed life.
That is why repentance matters.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) is commonly translated “repentance.”
It conveys a change of mind or understanding that, in its biblical setting, involves a decisive turning toward God and away from sin.
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what you were hiding.
It is not just being frightened by consequences.
It is turning to God in truth, trusting His mercy, and beginning to walk in obedience.
And no, genuine repentance does not mean you will never struggle again.
Christians still face temptation.
They still need confession.
They still need correction, growth, and the sustaining grace of God.
But there is a difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and deciding you no longer need to get up.
There is a difference between crying out for mercy and using the language of mercy to excuse deliberate rebellion.
Perhaps you know that difference more personally than you want to admit.
Perhaps there is something in your life you have been minimizing.
A habit you keep defending.
A relationship built on deception.
A resentment you refuse to surrender.
A secret compromise that has slowly reshaped your conscience.
Or perhaps your struggle is not a scandal visible to anyone else.
Perhaps you have simply grown cold.
You still believe the right things.
You still know the verses.
You still recognize the songs.
But somewhere along the way, prayer became rare, worship became mechanical, and the presence of God became less important to you than the approval of people.
You cannot remember the exact day it happened.
You only know you are not as close to Him as you once were.
And maybe that realization hurts.
If it does, do not turn that pain into another reason to hide.
Bring it to Christ.
Not because you can purchase His forgiveness through tears.
Not because your shame makes you worthy.
But because His mercy is sufficient, and His invitation to repent is real.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
There is no need to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
There is no need to expose private wounds to strangers.
You can come to God truthfully, even if the only words you can manage are:
“Lord, I have been drifting. Have mercy on me.”
He already knows what you are afraid to confess.
And the Gospel tells us that those who come to Christ in faith are not turned away.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
What an astonishing promise.
Ezekiel 23 shows the horror of covenant betrayal.
But Jesus reveals the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
And that is why we must not confuse the shocking language of judgment with the final word of the biblical story.
The final word for those who belong to Christ is not condemnation. It is redemption.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus...” — KJV
That is not a license to embrace sin.
It is the assurance that Christ has accomplished what guilty people could never accomplish for themselves.
The cross does not make sin insignificant.
The cross reveals both the gravity of sin and the greatness of divine love.
And the resurrection announces that death itself does not have the final victory.
So why did Ezekiel use language so shocking that many churches avoid reading it aloud?
Because the prophet was communicating the seriousness of Judah's covenant betrayal through a deliberately graphic allegory.
Because the people had repeatedly ignored warnings.
Because idolatry was not harmless religious experimentation.
Because their pursuit of foreign powers and false worship was leading toward national disaster.
Because religious privilege had not produced covenant faithfulness.
And because a people who had normalized their rebellion needed to hear an accusation they could not easily domesticate.
Yet we should not assume that the most graphic possible presentation is always the most faithful way to teach Scripture.
Pastors and teachers can address Ezekiel 23 honestly while exercising pastoral sensitivity, especially in mixed-age congregations and among people who have experienced sexual trauma.
Reverence for Scripture does not require sensationalism.
Sometimes faithfulness means explaining a difficult passage carefully rather than using its disturbing imagery to attract attention.
The goal is understanding, repentance, and renewed trust in God.
Not shock for its own sake.
And perhaps that is the challenge for us now.
Will we approach this chapter looking only for something scandalous?
Or will we allow its warning to confront our misplaced loyalties?
Will we use it to condemn people whose struggles are different from ours?
Or will we examine our own hearts before God?
Will we read its judgment and conclude that mercy has disappeared?
Or will we continue through Ezekiel until we hear God's promise to cleanse, renew, and restore?
Because the God who says, “I will give you a new heart,” is not asking us to repair our souls through religious performance.
He is calling us to receive the renewal that only He can give.
And through Jesus Christ, forgiveness and new life are not merely distant religious concepts.
They are the living hope of the Gospel.
That is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior.
Not a fascination with scandal.
Not a ministry built on humiliating the broken.
Not the idea that people must become impressive before they can approach God.
But a conviction that Scripture must be handled faithfully, Christ must remain central, and people must hear the truth about sin and the greater truth about the Savior who redeems sinners.
If this article made you examine something you have been avoiding, do not let the moment pass without bringing it before the Lord.
You might simply write, “Jesus, give me a new heart.”
Or “I’m still fighting. Pray for me.”
You do not have to disclose anything deeply personal. You can also share how Ezekiel 23 changed your understanding of idolatry, judgment, and grace.
Your honest reflection may encourage another believer who has been quietly struggling.
And think about someone you know who needs this message.
Someone who believes their past has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who has drifted away from faith.
Someone who is spiritually exhausted.
Someone who has been wounded by religion and needs to hear the Gospel presented with both truth and compassion.
That simple act can help sound biblical teaching reach people who might never enter a church building or open a Bible on their own.
Not because every difficult question has been answered here, but because Ezekiel 23 deserves more than a passing reaction.
Return to the chapter.
Read it in context.
Continue into Ezekiel 36 and 37.
Compare the prophetic warnings with the promises of restoration.
And keep asking how the whole counsel of Scripture directs us toward the holiness, justice, mercy, and saving work of God.
There is room here for serious questions, biblical learning, spiritual encouragement, and honest conversations about repentance and grace.
These resources are intended to make biblical learning more accessible, especially for people who want to grow but may not have the means to purchase a large collection of Christian books.
And if this ministry has helped you grow spiritually, I want to extend a personal invitation.
For believers who are able and willing to give, financial support can be one expression of generosity and stewardship.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It does not purchase God's favor.
And it should never replace your responsibilities to your family, local church, or people in genuine need.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That matters deeply.
Supporting Gospel ministry should come from willing generosity, not guilt or fear.
These products can serve as reminders of faith, tools for personal reflection, or thoughtful gifts for people you love.
It is helping make more Christ-centered teaching, biblical encouragement, and discipleship resources available to people who need them.
It is to follow Jesus.
Because the Gospel is bigger than a ministry.
The Gospel is the good news that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures.
It is the announcement that forgiveness is available through Him.
It is the call to repent, believe, and walk in the new life He gives.
And if you have spent years hiding behind appearances, perhaps today is the day to stop pretending.
If you have been chasing things that cannot satisfy your soul, perhaps today is the day to turn back.
If you have been using your past as evidence that God could never receive you, look again at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at the Savior who receives sinners and transforms lives.
Ezekiel 23 is disturbing because betrayal is serious.
Ezekiel 36 is beautiful because renewal is possible.
And the Gospel is glorious because Jesus Christ has accomplished the salvation that we could never earn.
The question is no longer merely why Ezekiel used such shocking language.
The question is what we will do with the truth it reveals.
Will we continue pushing God behind our backs?
Or will we turn toward the One who calls us to repentance and offers us life?
The most heartbreaking thing would not be discovering how far your heart has wandered, but hearing Christ call you home and deciding you would rather keep hiding.
